verses.verse:
काव्य प्रधानं च रसप्रधानं तालप्रधानं च स्वरप्रधानम्।
नाट्य प्रधानं च निबद्धगानम् भावप्रधानं त्वनिबद्ध गानम्।१३४।
verses.text: Singing where poetry leads, where rasa leads, where tāla leads, where svara leads and where drama leads is bound singing; singing where bhāva leads is unbound singing.

commentary.text: That is, a song in which the beauty of the poetry is greater and no special attention is paid to rāga and tāla is called kāvya-pradhāna (where poetry leads) singing, such as the Gīta Govinda and the like. Likewise, where the beauty of both poetry and notes together brings out some rasa (aesthetic flavour), as in ṭhumrī, ghazal and so on, it is called rasa-pradhāna (where rasa leads) singing; dhrupad, dhamār and so on are called tāla-pradhāna (where tāla leads), and khayāl svara-pradhāna (where svara leads); ālhā (ballad), nauṭaṅkī and the like, in which attention is kept on a story, are called nāṭya-pradhāna (where drama leads) singing. But singing in which there is no tāla at all, where ālāpa is done only with notes, or with notes helped by a few words, is called bhāva-pradhāna (where bhāva leads) anibaddha gāna (unbound, unmetred singing). So, apart from this, all the kinds above are called nibaddha gāna (bound, metred singing).

For nibaddha gāna (bound singing), it would be proper to practise speaking and writing syllables counted in their natural mātrās (beats). So now attend to the following rules for the natural mātrās of syllables.
A short syllable has one mātrā; a long syllable has two mātrās.
A syllable with anusvāra or visarga, and one that comes before a conjunct, counts as long.

That is, a short syllable is to be taken as of one mātrā and a long syllable as of two mātrās. A syllable with anusvāra or visarga is also to be taken as of two mātrās, and a short syllable that comes before a conjunct letter should also be taken as long, of two mātrās. The method of writing and reading them in music notation is as follows.

commentary.text: In this way the mātrās of words should be counted in their natural form when writing and reading. But in some places, as exceptions, people also sing e, o, ai and au short, e.g. - te re – me – re –. ek rā – t meṃ. hamā – rā ha mā – rā – - and so on. To gain knowledge of these subtle elements of music, contact with a guru, with a pure mind, is necessary. On the basis of the rule above, every caupāī of the Rāmāyaṇa will be of 32 mātrās.
In nibaddha gāna (bound singing) the sam (first beat of the cycle) is of great importance, so we cannot go further without understanding the definition of sam.
